papers.title: Grounding User Preferences in Shared Multimodal Concepts for Recommendation
papers.authors: Ao Xu, Jinhui Huang, Wenqiang Tang, Tiehua Mei, Hongru Hou, Hengrui Chen, Jiaqing Liang, Deqing Yang
papers.summary: Multimodal recommenders now describe items in fine visual and textual detail, but user preferences are still often tied to individual items, so recurring factors such as style and atmosphere have no shared identity, and similar evidence from different items is hard to accumulate. MKGE induces an addressable concept vocabulary from posters and titles, and grounds each user's history in those concepts. It then jointly models direct user-item evidence and preference signals that travel through concepts, so evidence from different items can accumulate around the same factors. Concept induction can run offline, and online ranking uses only the trained graph model. On three public benchmarks, it outperforms collaborative, knowledge-graph, multimodal, and recent language-model recommenders on all six reported metrics. On MovieLens-1M, relative to removing the user-concept graph, the gain for low-activity users reaches 24.74%, and that advantage shrinks as activity rises.
papers.abstract: Multimodal recommendation has substantially advanced item understanding by incorporating rich visual and textual content. Yet user preferences are still commonly encoded as implicit signals tied to individual items, leaving recurring semantic factors without persistent identities that can be shared across items. We introduce MKGE, a multimodal knowledge graph framework that represents these factors as canonical, addressable concepts. MKGE induces a domain-adaptive concept vocabulary from item images and titles, grounds each user's interaction history in supported concepts, and jointly models direct user-item evidence and concept-mediated preference signals. By turning recurring semantics into shared coordinates, MKGE enables evidence from different items to accumulate around the same preference factors. Extensive experiments on three public benchmarks demonstrate that MKGE consistently outperforms collaborative, knowledge-graph, multimodal, and recent LLM/MLLM-based recommenders across all six reported metrics. Controlled studies further demonstrate the importance of canonical concept identities and personalized user-concept correspondence, with especially pronounced gains over removing or rewiring the user graph for low-activity users. These results establish canonical multimodal concepts as effective units for preference modeling and transfer. Code, constructed knowledge graphs, and prompts are available at https://github.com/Garden1a-X/MKGE.

venue.name: WSDM
venue.label: WSDM 2027
venue.evidence: Accepted at WSDM 2027 (Main Conference). 10 pages, 7 figures, 6 tables

scenario: Today's generative-recommendation lineup has a single paper, and it is less about stuffing multimodal features into a user vector than about giving recurring factors such as style and atmosphere a shared, addressable identity. The method induces a concept vocabulary from posters and titles, grounds user history in those concepts, and uses both direct interactions and preference signals that travel through concepts. The concepts can be built offline, so serving need not call a large model. All six metrics improve on three public benchmarks, with larger gains for low-activity users, because the same concept can accumulate evidence from different items when a single item provides too little signal. For generative and multimodal recommenders, a user's taste need not remain tied only to the few items already seen.
